title: Weekly links September 4: listening, how to not make your AI RCT useless, many conference calls, and more…
gist: A weekly links roundup for development economists flags a rapid rise in AI-focused randomized controlled trials (RCTs) registered via the AEA registry, warns these risk becoming obsolete 'one-and-done' studies given how fast AI evolves, and notes AI-based peer review (Refine.ink) is being adopted as a formal pre-publication audit step by the American Economic Association and Econometric Society.

insights.claim: AEA registry data analyzed by Tim Ohlenburg and co-authors on VoxDev shows the number of AI-focused randomized controlled trials in the research pipeline is growing rapidly.
insights.speaker: David McKenzie
insights.so_what: A surge in AI RCTs signals academia is racing to generate causal evidence on AI's development impact, but the studies' relevance window may be short given how fast the technology changes.
insights.locator: On VoxDev, Tim Ohlenburg and co-authors use AEA registry data

insights.claim: Because AI technology evolves and is adopted so quickly, there is a risk of a wave of 'one-and-done' RCTs in low- and middle-income countries whose results are outdated before publication, fail to generalize, and are never taken up by governments or scaled.
insights.speaker: David McKenzie
insights.so_what: Investors and funders backing AI-for-development research or evaluation firms should discount findings from single, narrow AI RCTs and favor designs built for durability/generalizability.
insights.quote: In a worst-case scenario, we could see a wave of one-and-done research projects in LMICs, that are out of date before the results are public, don't generalise, and aren't taken up by governments or scale
insights.locator: discuss the challenges in randomizing a rapidly evolving

themes.theme: AI enters the research process itself

insights.claim: Refine.ink, an AI-based review tool, will now be used by both the American Economic Association and the Econometric Society as a final pre-publication audit of a paper's technical execution and exposition.
insights.speaker: David McKenzie
insights.so_what: Formal institutional adoption of AI-refereeing by top economics bodies is a concrete data point on AI penetrating professional/scientific gatekeeping functions, not just industry workflows.

insights.claim: Economic Innovation Group featured Chad Syverson discussing current evidence on AI's effects on productivity and employment, including how mismeasurement of intangible assets can distort the observed productivity picture.
insights.speaker: David McKenzie
insights.so_what: Flags measurement of intangible assets as a specific methodological blind spot that could be understating AI's true productivity contribution in official statistics.
insights.locator: the Economic Innovation Group has Chad Syverson give his take

themes.theme: Methodology critique: what economics chooses to measure

insights.claim: Biju Rao argues that economics' focus on what is measurable via survey modules systematically excludes important aspects of subjects' lives, calling this exclusion the discipline's central problem rather than a mere methodological convenience.
insights.speaker: David McKenzie
insights.so_what: A methodological critique worth noting for anyone relying on survey-based development/impact data: it may systemically miss non-quantifiable but material factors in subjects' welfare.
insights.quote: Economics tends to focus on the measurable, which can exclude what is important; if it cannot be included in a survey module, it is not worth studying.
insights.locator: Biju Rao in In Development magazine on
